overview: Japan is one of the safest destinations in the world for travellers. The biggest health-safety topics to know are prescription-drug rules (surprisingly strict), natural hazards (earthquakes and typhoons), and summer heat. Street crime is rare but petty scams do exist around some nightlife districts.

emergency_numbers.label: Japan Helpline (24/7 English)
emergency_numbers.notes: General information, medical and legal triage.

hazards.title: Earthquakes
hazards.body: Small quakes are felt several times a month. Larger ones are rare but possible. Buildings in Japan are engineered for this.
hazards.what_to_do: If you feel shaking, drop, cover under a sturdy table, and hold on. Do not run outside during the shake — falling debris is the bigger risk. Afterwards, leave gas and electricity alone and wait for the NERV Disaster Prevention app or local PA announcements.

hazards.title: Typhoons
hazards.body: Typhoon season peaks August-October. A typical typhoon shuts trains and flights for 12-24 hours.
hazards.what_to_do: Track on NERV or the JMA app. If a strong typhoon is forecast, buy food and water a day ahead, charge devices, and keep plans flexible. Airlines usually waive rebooking fees 24-48 hours ahead.

hazards.title: Tsunami
hazards.body: Coastal risk after a large offshore earthquake. Central Tokyo is inland; seaside towns are the higher risk.
hazards.what_to_do: After a strong quake near the coast, head for higher ground immediately — follow signs with a wave icon. Do not wait for sirens.

hazards.title: Summer heat
hazards.body: July-August highs regularly reach 33-37 °C with 70%+ humidity.
hazards.what_to_do: Carry water, use a cooling towel, plan indoor breaks every 90 minutes, and slow down. Konbini sell ice-cold Pocari Sweat and ¥100 hand fans. Ambulances respond to heatstroke in minutes.

hazards.title: Crime & scams
hazards.body: Street theft is rare; violent crime against tourists is very rare. Be cautious of touts in Roppongi and Kabukicho who lure visitors into overpriced bars — walk past, don't follow.
hazards.what_to_do: Stick to venues you looked up in advance. If your wallet or phone is lost, go to the nearest kōban (neighborhood police box) — Japan has one of the world's best lost-and-found rates.

prohibited_meds.summary: Japan restricts several common Western medications. Pseudoephedrine (Sudafed, Vicks inhalers, some Claritin-D), Adderall, and some cough syrups are entirely banned — bringing them in, even with a prescription, can result in confiscation and legal trouble.
watchlist: CBD products not made from approved extract
prohibited_meds.allowed_without_cert: Up to 1 month supply of most OTC and prescription medicines (2 months for prescriptions if not on the watchlist).
prohibited_meds.yakkan_shoumei_note: If you need a larger supply, insulin injectors, CPAP, or any watchlist drug, apply for a Yakkan Shoumei import certificate at least 2-3 weeks before travel. It's free.

pharmacies.name: Matsumoto Kiyoshi
pharmacies.notes: Largest drugstore chain; many have prescription counters.

pharmacies.name: Welcia / Tomod's
pharmacies.notes: Stocks Western-brand OTC pain relievers (Tylenol, Advil).

pharmacies.name: AMDA International Medical Information Center
pharmacies.notes: English-speaking hotline to find English-friendly clinics. Phone: 03-6233-9266.

tap_water: Tap water is safe throughout Japan. Public drinking fountains are common in parks and stations. Refill bottles at konbini ice machines or temple water pavilions.

lgbtq.country_legal_status: Same-sex relationships are legal. Same-sex marriage is not yet recognised nationally, but many Tokyo wards and 300+ municipalities issue 'partnership certificates' with limited rights.
lgbtq.city_tolerance: Tokyo is one of the most LGBTQ-comfortable cities in East Asia. Public displays of affection from any couple are uncommon across the board — keep things low-key in general.
safe_neighborhoods: Shinjuku Ni-chome (Asia's densest queer nightlife district)

dietary_cards.label: Vegan (no animal products)
dietary_cards.jp_text: 私はヴィーガンです。肉、魚、卵、乳製品、だし(魚介スープ)を食べられません。料理に使われていないか確認していただけますか？
dietary_cards.en_gloss: I am vegan. I cannot eat meat, fish, eggs, dairy, or dashi (fish broth). Could you please check none of these are used in the dish?

dietary_cards.label: Vegetarian (no meat or fish)
dietary_cards.jp_text: 私はベジタリアンです。肉と魚を食べられません。だし(魚介スープ)も含まれていないか確認してください。
dietary_cards.en_gloss: I am vegetarian. I cannot eat meat or fish. Please also check there is no dashi (fish broth).

dietary_cards.label: Halal (no pork / no alcohol in cooking)
dietary_cards.jp_text: 私はイスラム教徒です。豚肉、豚由来の調味料(例: とんこつ)、みりん、料理酒などのアルコールを食べられません。
dietary_cards.en_gloss: I am Muslim. I cannot eat pork, pork-derived ingredients (e.g. tonkotsu broth), mirin, or cooking alcohol.

dietary_cards.label: Gluten-free (celiac / wheat allergy)
dietary_cards.jp_text: 小麦とグルテンのアレルギーがあります。醤油やうどん、ラーメン、天ぷらなど小麦を含む食品は食べられません。
dietary_cards.en_gloss: I have a wheat/gluten allergy. I cannot eat soy sauce, udon, ramen, tempura, or any food containing wheat.

dietary_cards.label: Peanut allergy
dietary_cards.jp_text: ピーナッツアレルギーがあります。ピーナッツや落花生を使わない料理をお願いします。
dietary_cards.en_gloss: I have a peanut allergy. Please serve me food with no peanuts.

solo_notes: Solo travel is extremely comfortable for all genders. Late-night return via train or taxi from entertainment districts like Shibuya, Shinjuku, Roppongi is routine. The only area where solo travellers sometimes report harassment is on very crowded rush-hour trains; women-only cars are marked pink on some lines during peak hours.
